title: The Isthmus for Rent: the Informant, the Comandancia, and the Ten Days in the Nunciature
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Panama City, the birth without a settled year
stops.date_confidence: unsettled. Sources give 1934, 1936 and 1938 for the birth year; the obituaries of May 2017 report his age at death as eighty-three, which fits 1934. The day is carried from the research pool and is not independently confirmed here.
stops.campa: In a poor district of the capital a son is born to a family that keeps no papers worth contesting. His mother dies of tuberculosis while he is small and a godmother raises him. Three years are offered for the birth and no document decides between them, so the man who will spend his life inside intelligence files begins outside every file. Panama in this decade is a country with a canal through the middle of it belonging to another country, and the Zone that holds the canal is foreign soil a walk from the barrio.
suggested_refs: Panama City civil registers for 1934, 1936 and 1938, none of which has been produced by any source
sources: Noriega with Peter Eisner, America's Prisoner (1997), catalogue record only

stops.name: La Chorrera, the other birthplace
stops.date_confidence: the same disputed year as the capital claim. The two birthplaces are alternatives, not stages of one journey, and the atlas pins both rather than choosing.
stops.campa: Thirty kilometres west of the capital stands the town that several biographical accounts give as his actual birthplace, against the memoir and against the reference works. No primary document has settled the question either way. The press profiles that carried La Chorrera through 1988 and 1989 named no register and no baptismal entry, and the memoir that names the city was written by a man with a case to make. Both towns are kept here rather than choosing between them. Nothing reached in this research places the birth in either one on a dated page.
suggested_refs: Contemporary press profiles of 1988-1990 giving La Chorrera as the birthplace, none citing a register
sources: Noriega, America's Prisoner (1997), which gives Panama City

stops.name: Santa Ana, the Instituto Nacional
stops.date_confidence: circa. Secondary accounts place him at the school in the years around 1947 to 1953 without giving an entry or a leaving date; month and day default to the first of January.
stops.campa: At the foot of Cerro Ancon, fronting the avenue that will later take the name of the martyrs, stands the country's most prestigious public secondary school, the forge of Panama's political and military elite for a century. The boy from the barrio is inside it. His classmates are sons of the families that run the republic. What he does between leaving these classrooms and arriving in Lima is documented nowhere this research could reach, and five years of a life are simply missing from the record.
suggested_refs: The Instituto Nacional de Panama on Avenida de los Martires, Santa Ana

stops.name: Panama City, the first payment
stops.date_confidence: year attested through United States federal prosecutors' documentation of thirty-one years of payments; no month or day is recorded, so both default to the first.
stops.campa: A teenager takes ten dollars and seventy cents from United States intelligence and the relationship begins. Federal prosecutors will one day count thirty-one years of such payments. He is an informant before he is a cadet, and a cadet before he is an officer. He will spend the next three decades collecting a second salary that never once appears on a Panamanian payroll, and that outlasts four different presidents of the country paying it.
suggested_refs: United States federal prosecution exhibits documenting thirty-one years of payments to Noriega
sources: Wikipedia, 'Manuel Noriega', citing the federal prosecution record

stops.name: Lima, the Escuela Militar de Chorrillos
stops.date_confidence: the training runs 1958 to 1962; the commission as second lieutenant in the Panamanian National Guard is attested for 1962. Month and day default to the first.
stops.campa: He crosses a continent to become a soldier, studying engineering as a cadet at Peru's military academy on the shore south of Lima. Here, according to the payment records declassified decades later and to Dinges, the informant is formally recruited, and the arrangement that began with ten dollars and seventy cents becomes a career running parallel to the uniform. He returns and is commissioned a second lieutenant in the National Guard in 1962. Two payrolls, one man, from the first day he holds a rank.
suggested_refs: The Escuela Militar de Chorrillos, Lima; declassified CIA and DIA payment records released in the 1990s

stops.name: Fort Gulick, the School of the Americas
stops.date_confidence: contested. The research pool gives 1966 in one lens and 1967 in another, neither citing a document. The atlas pins 1967 and leaves the discrepancy standing; month and day default to the first.
stops.campa: In the Canal Zone, on soil that is legally not Panama, the United States Army runs a school for Latin American officers. Noriega takes counterintelligence training at Fort Gulick. The instruction and the network both go home with him: the men he meets in these classrooms will staff the services he later runs, and the American officers who teach him keep his file open. Three years after this he is chief of Panamanian military intelligence, compiling files of his own on the dissidents, businessmen and foreign officials of his country.
suggested_refs: United States Army School of the Americas enrollment records, Fort Gulick, Canal Zone

stops.name: David, Chiriqui: the province secured
stops.date_confidence: the coup falls on 11 October 1968; his work in Chiriqui runs through 1968 and 1969 and the pin takes the coup's date.
stops.campa: The National Guard overthrows President Arnulfo Arias and Omar Torrijos takes the country. In the western province against the Costa Rican border, Noriega puts down what resistance there is and hands Chiriqui to Torrijos intact. The reward is military intelligence. He does not appear on the balcony in the photographs of the new government. He is the officer who keeps the file on everyone who does. Torrijos rules Panama for thirteen years and Noriega keeps the files for eleven of them.
suggested_refs: The National Guard coup of 11 October 1968 against Arnulfo Arias

stops.name: El Chorrillo, the G-2
stops.date_confidence: the promotion to lieutenant colonel and the appointment as chief of the G-2 are attested for 1970; no day is recorded and the pin's coordinates are approximate to the garrison district.
stops.campa: Lieutenant colonel, chief of military intelligence of the National Guard. From the garrison district he builds the directorate that is the real base of everything after: files on dissidents, on businessmen, on foreign officials, on the officers standing above him in the chain of command. The Kerry Committee will describe the operation in 1988 and the Miami trial record in 1992. Nineteen years from this date United States artillery burns this ground and the wooden tenements around it, and the quarter is still called El Chorrillo.
suggested_refs: The Comandancia and the G-2 directorate in El Chorrillo, Panama City

stops.name: Langley, the payroll
stops.date_confidence: the year the CIA places him on the regular payroll is attested through the federal prosecution record. The further claim that George H. W. Bush personally approved his continued status in 1976 rests on FOIA correspondence not re-fetched in this pass and is carried as reconstruction.
stops.campa: The agency puts him on the regular payroll. The arrangement survives Nixon, Ford, Carter and Reagan, and it survives the accumulation of trafficking evidence in the same building's own files. Bush is Director of Central Intelligence in 1976 and is said to have signed off on keeping him; that correspondence is FOIA material this research did not obtain, so it is carried here as tradition rather than fact. Bush's own role in keeping him on the payroll remains an allegation the files have not yet been made to confirm.
suggested_refs: Declassified CIA correspondence on Noriega's asset status, released under FOIA in the 1990s
sources: Wikipedia, 'Manuel Noriega', citing the federal prosecution record
QUEUE.md, George H. W. Bush entry

stops.name: Cerro Marta, Cocle: the plane comes down
stops.date_confidence: attested for the crash. That the crash was sabotage is contested tradition and carries no proof; the officially recorded cause remains weather.
stops.campa: Omar Torrijos dies when his small plane goes into the Cocle highlands. The official cause is weather. Critics of the man who benefits say sabotage; no investigation has proved it, and the tradition does not go away for that. Noriega is among the colonels next in the chain of command. Within two years the rivals are gone and the National Guard has become the Panama Defense Forces with him at the head of it. The accusation is recorded here as an accusation, and the crash as a crash.
suggested_refs: The Cocle highlands crash site of Omar Torrijos, 31 July 1981

stops.name: Calle 50, the accounts at BCCI
stops.date_confidence: the accounts run across the 1980s; 1982 is the earliest year the research pool assigns to the Panama City branch relationship, and month and day default to the first.
stops.campa: In the banking district he keeps accounts at the Bank of Credit and Commerce International, Agha Hasan Abedi's institution, the bank regulators will close across seventy countries in 1991. Amjad Awan, who heads the Panama branch, handles the relationship with Syed A. Hussain. Through these accounts United States investigators later trace drug proceeds and covert payments alike, moving through the same pipes and distinguishable only by paperwork. Abedi's own bank will collapse under multinational regulators within a decade, taking much of that paper trail down with it.
suggested_refs: The BCCI Panama branch records entered in evidence in US v. Noriega
sources: Wikipedia, 'Bank of Credit and Commerce International'
US Senate Kerry Committee report on BCCI, 1992
US v. Noriega trial record, S.D. Fla.

stops.name: Panama City, commander of the Defense Forces
stops.date_confidence: attested.
stops.campa: He becomes de facto ruler of Panama as commander of the Panama Defense Forces, the National Guard renamed and enlarged. He does not take the presidency. Presidents are appointed and removed beneath him for the next six years while the command stays where it is. The intelligence chief has become the state, and the country's working constitution is the filing system he built in 1970. Six years from this date, on this same stretch of the capital, the invasion that ends it begins.
suggested_refs: The founding of the Panama Defense Forces from the National Guard, 1983
sources: arthur_ben.journey.json for the shared Panama City pin

stops.name: Coclesito, the farm in the forest
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. DEA debriefings cited in the 1988 Kerry Committee report place cartel meetings at the farmstead around 1983 and 1984; Noriega's memoir denies them, no meeting site is independently confirmed, and month and day default to the first.
stops.campa: At the jungle farmstead Torrijos kept, associates of Pablo Escobar's Medellin cartel are reported to meet Panamanian intermediaries close to Noriega, to arrange transshipment and the protection of refining. The debriefings that say so reach the record through a Senate committee; the memoir denies it flatly. What is not disputed is the geography: a country narrow enough to cross in a morning, lying between the largest cocaine producer on earth and its largest market, with a farmstead in the trees between them.
suggested_refs: DEA debriefings on Medellin cartel meetings in Panama, cited in the Kerry Committee report, 1988
sources: Noriega, America's Prisoner (1997), which denies direct cartel meetings
OpenStreetMap for the location of Coclesito

stops.name: Panama City, the count corrected
stops.date_confidence: month only. The research pool gives May 1984 for the election and no day; the day defaults to the first.
stops.campa: Panama votes for a president for the first time in sixteen years. The opposition appears to win. Noriega manipulates the count and Nicolas Ardito Barletta is installed. Fraud enters Panamanian politics as arithmetic rather than as accusation, and it will be there again in 1989, done more crudely and filmed. The count is done by men who answer to the Defense Forces. Nothing in the republic's paperwork obliges the commander of those forces to hold any office at all.
suggested_refs: The Panamanian presidential election of May 1984 and the installation of Nicolas Ardito Barletta

stops.name: Colon, the free zone at the other mouth
stops.date_confidence: the free zone's role as a laundering point is documented across 1982 to 1989; the pin's date is arbitrary within that span and month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: At the Caribbean end of the canal the free trade zone moves containers and currency under controls investigators later call negligent. Cartel proceeds are washed here, and the trial record of 1992 sets Noriega's personal cut of trafficking fees beside the zone's traffic. The same accounts at BCCI's Panama branch that carry his cut carry this zone's currency too, distinguishable from ordinary trade only by the destination of the wire.
suggested_refs: The Colon Free Trade Zone in the 1980s; the Hotel Washington, Colon
sources: US v. Noriega trial record, S.D. Fla. 1992
DEA reporting cited in the Kerry Committee report

stops.name: Ilopango, the resupply base
stops.date_confidence: the Contra resupply flights through Ilopango are documented for 1985 and 1986; the pin takes the earlier year and defaults month and day.
stops.campa: The air base outside San Salvador is the hub of the Contra resupply pipeline. Panamanian territory and Panamanian intelligence services help it work, and in exchange Washington tolerates what Noriega does with the rest of his country. Oliver North and William Casey run the operation from the other end, coordinating through channels Noriega's own services keep open. The Kerry Committee publishes the outline in 1988, the same year two federal grand juries indict the man who made the isthmus available.
suggested_refs: Ilopango air base and the Contra resupply pipeline, 1985-1986
sources: QUEUE.md, Oliver North and William Casey entries

stops.name: Paso Canoas, the road from Costa Rica
stops.date_confidence: month only. The research pool gives September 1985 for the detention and the killing and no day, so the day defaults to the first. The pin is the border crossing and is approximate; the body was found on the Costa Rican side.
stops.campa: Hugo Spadafora, who fought under Torrijos and has said publicly that Noriega protects traffickers, crosses from Costa Rica and is taken by Noriega's forces. His decapitated body is found on the Costa Rican side of the line, in a post office bag. An intercepted telephone call carries Luis Cordoba's report to Noriega, 'We have the rabid dog,' and the answer prosecutors will read as an order. He is convicted of conspiracy in the killing in absentia, after his fall, and serves that sentence in Panama a quarter of a century later.
stops.quote: And what does one do with a dog that has rabies?
stops.quote_source: Manuel Noriega, reply to Luis Cordoba in an NSA-intercepted telephone call, September 1985; quoted per R. M. Koster and Guillermo Sanchez Borbon, In the Time of the Tyrants: Panama, 1968-1990, cited in Wikipedia, 'Manuel Noriega'
suggested_refs: The NSA intercept of the Cordoba call, cited by Koster and Sanchez Borbon
sources: Koster and Sanchez Borbon, In the Time of the Tyrants (1990), at second hand

stops.name: Leadenhall Street, the head office
stops.date_confidence: the London head office oversees the correspondent network throughout the 1980s; the pin's year is arbitrary within that span and month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: The bank's principal London office sits in the City, running the correspondent network through which money from the Panama branch reaches everywhere else. In 1991 regulators close BCCI across seventy countries, and the Senate publishes the anatomy the year after. The artist Mark Lombardi will draw this network as arcs and nodes, with Abedi and Clark Clifford and North and Casey inside it. Noriega is one node on a diagram nobody has drawn yet.
suggested_refs: BCCI's principal London office, Leadenhall Street; Mark Lombardi's BCCI-ICIC-FAB drawings
sources: US Senate Kerry Committee report on BCCI, 1992
QUEUE.md, Mark Lombardi and Clark Clifford entries

stops.name: The Darien Gap, the corridor
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The corridor's use through the 1980s is broadly attested in DEA field reporting cited by the Kerry Committee; specific waypoints inside Darien are not, and the pin's year is arbitrary.
stops.campa: Between Panama and Colombia the road stops and the forest begins, and cocaine moves through it overland and along both coasts. The route is attested; the waypoints inside it are reconstruction, and that uncertainty is stated here rather than papered over with an invented line. The gap has swallowed armies and colonies before: nothing built across it has ever lasted, and nothing moving through it has ever been easy to track. The traffic Noriega taxes is only the latest thing to use that ungoverned door.
suggested_refs: DEA field reporting on the Darien corridor cited in the Kerry Committee report, 1988

stops.name: Panama City, the march of a hundred thousand
stops.date_confidence: attested.
stops.campa: An estimated hundred thousand people march against him in the capital. The Defense Forces meet the crowds and the crowds come back. After this summer the regime holds its own capital by force and governs nothing. Washington, which has kept him on a payroll for sixteen years, begins reading the files it paid for as a liability rather than an asset. Nothing that follows surprises anyone in either capital, which does not stop it taking two and a half more years to arrive.
suggested_refs: The Panama City protests of June 1987 and the Cruzada Civilista

stops.name: Miami, the indictment
stops.date_confidence: month only. The research pool gives February 1988 for the grand jury indictments in Miami and Tampa; the day defaults to the first.
stops.campa: Federal grand juries in Miami and in Tampa indict the sitting ruler of a foreign country on drug trafficking and racketeering, alleging he was paid to let Colombian cocaine cross Panama toward the United States. He has been on the American payroll for seventeen years and an informant for thirty-three. Both facts sit in the files of the same government. This courthouse convicts him four years later, after an army has been sent to collect him from a Vatican mission at the other end of the isthmus.
suggested_refs: The February 1988 federal indictments of Noriega in the Southern and Middle Districts of Florida
sources: Department of Justice indictment reporting, February 1988

stops.name: Panama City, the beating after the rally
stops.date_confidence: attested for 11 May. The election falls on 7 May, the annulment on 10 May, and the beating the following day. The street is named by no source reached: the pin is a central-city approximation and Via Espana should not be treated as verified.
stops.campa: The opposition wins decisively and Noriega voids the result. The next day his Dignity Battalions catch Guillermo Endara and Guillermo Ford coming away from a rally. Endara is struck with an iron club and takes eight stitches. Ford, the vice-presidential candidate, is photographed in a white guayabera soaked red, still on his feet and still being hit, and the picture travels around the world inside a day. Seven months later Endara is sworn in as president of Panama on a United States military base.
suggested_refs: Wire photographs of the beating of Guillermo Ford, 11 May 1989

stops.name: Casco Viejo, the veterans before the invasion
stops.date_confidence: the delegation is placed in the autumn before the invasion; Pete Zastrow of the VVAW national office is documented in Panama at the end of November. The September date is inherited byte for byte from arthur_ben.journey.json, which carries the delegation stop.
stops.campa: A Vietnam Veterans Against the War delegation comes to Panama to watch the confrontation between Washington and Noriega from inside the country, and to sit with Panamanians who do not want an invasion. Pete Zastrow writes of being here at the end of November, and a Panamanian eyewitness thanks the veterans for standing with them beforehand. Arthur Ben is said by his family to have been on that delegation. No published source names him on it, and his presence here is recorded as exactly that claim and no more.
suggested_refs: Pete Zastrow in The Veteran, Summer 1990, vol 20 no 2; Lamoin Werlein-Jaen's eyewitness report
sources: Pete Zastrow, The Veteran, Summer 1990, vvaw.org/content/?id=2961

stops.name: El Chorrillo, Giroldi's hours
stops.date_confidence: attested. The rank is Lieutenant Colonel; one lens of the research pool called Giroldi a Major and its own chronology contradicted it.
stops.campa: Lieutenant Colonel Moises Giroldi Vera leads junior officers of the Defense Forces against the commander inside the Comandancia itself, and holds him briefly. Loyal troops break the rising the same day. The captured rebels are tortured and executed, Giroldi among them. Seventy-eight days later United States artillery burns this building and the wooden neighbourhood around it, and the officers who might have removed Noriega from inside the Panamanian army are already dead by his own order.
suggested_refs: The failed Giroldi coup of 3 October 1989 inside the Comandancia

stops.name: Panama City, Maximum Leader
stops.date_confidence: attested for the resolution. Its Spanish text could not be traced to a primary transcript in this research, and what circulates in its place is the American president's characterization of it.
stops.campa: The National Assembly names him Maximum Leader and head of government and declares that a state of war exists between Panama and the United States. The wording of that resolution could not be traced to a primary transcript here, and what circulates instead is Washington's account of what it said, which is a different document with a different author. The distinction decides who is understood to have declared the war, and it is kept marked as untraced here rather than resolved by borrowing the paraphrase.
suggested_refs: Asamblea Nacional de Representantes de Corregimientos, resolution of 15 December 1989, Spanish text not located
sources: American Presidency Project, Bush address of 20 December 1989

stops.name: El Chorrillo, the roadblock
stops.date_confidence: attested for the day; the pin is approximate to the garrison district rather than to the roadblock itself, whose location is not given in the sources reached.
stops.campa: United States Marine First Lieutenant Robert Paz is shot dead at a Defense Forces roadblock in the capital. A United States naval officer and his wife are detained and harassed the same night. Four days later the president of the United States names both incidents in the address announcing that an invasion is already under way. The casus belli exists and so does the invasion plan, which has been drawn for months and carries the name Blue Spoon until somebody in Washington considers how it will read in a newspaper.
suggested_refs: The killing of 1st Lt Robert Paz at a PDF roadblock, 16 December 1989

stops.name: Panama City, twelve forty-six in the morning
stops.date_confidence: attested to the hour.
stops.campa: At twelve forty-six in the morning the United States invades Panama with more than twenty-seven thousand troops and three hundred aircraft. The operation is called Just Cause; the plan was called Blue Spoon until the name was judged for print. Noriega does not fall that night, and it will take two more weeks, an aircraft on an apron and a burning quarter before he does. Arthur Ben's own account of the war names this hour and this city, from the far side of the delegation that had tried to head it off.
stops.quote: Last Friday, Noriega declared his military dictatorship to be in a state of war with the United States and publicly threatened the lives of Americans in Panama.
stops.quote_source: George H. W. Bush, Address to the Nation Announcing United States Military Action in Panama, 20 December 1989; transcript, American Presidency Project
suggested_refs: Bush's address to the nation of 20 December 1989, presidency.ucsb.edu

stops.name: Punta Paitilla, the aircraft on the apron
stops.date_confidence: attested for the opening hours of the operation.
stops.campa: Navy SEALs assault the small airport inside the city in the first minutes of the operation, to destroy Noriega's private jet and close the air to him. They take heavy casualties on open ground doing it. The aircraft is disabled and the man is not there. For the rest of that day and for four days after it, an army of twenty-seven thousand holds a country of two million and cannot locate one person inside it. The operation keeps that shape until Christmas Eve.
suggested_refs: The SEAL assault on Punta Paitilla Airport, 20 December 1989, and its casualty review
sources: US Department of Defense after-action reports

stops.name: El Chorrillo, the quarter burns
stops.date_confidence: attested for the day. The civilian death toll is contested and is not resolved by the atlas.
stops.campa: The Comandancia is bombarded and burned. The wooden tenements packed around the garrison catch, and the fire takes the neighbourhood. Official counts give roughly three hundred and fourteen Panamanian soldiers and two hundred and two civilians dead across the whole operation; independent and Panamanian estimates run to about three thousand. Twenty-three American servicemen are killed and three hundred and twenty-five wounded. Thousands who lived in El Chorrillo are homeless by morning, and the two sets of numbers have never been reconciled.
suggested_refs: Physicians for Human Rights, Operation Just Cause: the human cost (1991)
sources: New York Times and Miami Herald reporting, December 1989

stops.name: Fort Clayton, a president sworn in on a base
stops.date_confidence: attested for the day. The coordinates are approximate to the former Canal Zone base.
stops.campa: Guillermo Endara, whose victory Noriega annulled seven months earlier and who was beaten in the street for it, takes the oath as president of Panama at a United States military installation while the shooting is still going on and before anyone knows where Noriega is. The election of May is honoured on the twentieth of December, on a base, by an army from another country. The Defense Forces will be dissolved and Panama will keep no army after this.
suggested_refs: The swearing-in of Guillermo Endara at a US installation, 20 December 1989

stops.name: Altos del Golf, the house without him
stops.date_confidence: attested for the day. The pin is neighbourhood-level; the exact address of the residence is not documented in the sources reached.
stops.campa: Soldiers go through his residence within hours and find pornography, ritual paraphernalia and cash, and American officials make sure the inventory is published. They do not find Noriega. For four days nobody can say where he is. The inventory of his shelves runs in the newspapers instead, filling the space in the coverage that a capture was meant to fill. He is somewhere in the same city, under a reward of one million dollars, moving between houses.
suggested_refs: Press inventories of the raid on Noriega's residence, December 1989
sources: Contemporaneous Associated Press and Reuters reporting, December 1989

stops.name: Ancon, the Apostolic Nunciature
stops.date_confidence: attested for 24 December, ten days before the surrender. The coordinates are contested: the research pool gave this building two positions 1.3 km apart and OpenStreetMap gives a third for the present-day nunciature, which is the value used here and in the following stops. Nothing reached establishes where the 1989 building stood.
stops.campa: On Christmas Eve he walks into the diplomatic mission of the Holy See and asks for refuge, and the Vatican gives it. American troops ring the compound, and Washington writes to Rome that an indictment for drug trafficking is an exception to diplomatic immunity. Loud rock and roll music is played at the building day and night, in a densely populated quarter, while the negotiation runs on inside it. The National Security Adviser of the United States, looking back, gives that part of the operation its name.
stops.quote: a low moment in U.S. Army history
stops.quote_source: Brent Scowcroft, National Security Advisor, on the loud-music harassment of the Nunciature; quoted in Meena Bose and Rosanna Perotti, From Cold War to New World Order (Greenwood Press, 2002), p. 181
suggested_refs: The siege of the Apostolic Nunciature, 24 December 1989 to 3 January 1990

stops.name: Ancon, the surrender
stops.date_confidence: attested.
stops.campa: After ten days inside, the Papal Nuncio Sebastian Laboa talks him out. Laboa tells the press afterward that he is better at psychology than at anything else. Archbishop Marcos McGrath of Panama, who sees him that evening, calls him a broken man. He comes out of his room in a crisp tan general's uniform with four stars and gives himself up at the gate. He is taken into custody as a prisoner of war under the Geneva Conventions, a status the United States will later set aside in favour of treating him as a criminal defendant. That night he writes to his wife Felicidad.
stops.quote: I go now on an adventure.
stops.quote_source: Manuel Noriega, letter to his wife Felicidad written the night of his surrender; quoted in Kevin Buckley, Panama: The Whole Story, p. 247
suggested_refs: Time, 'A Guest Who Wore Out His Welcome,' 15 January 1990

stops.name: Howard Air Force Base, the flight out
stops.date_confidence: attested for the night of 3 January; the aircraft lands in Florida on the fourth.
stops.campa: He is driven to the air base in the old Canal Zone and flown out of Panama the same night, ending four decades in the country. Operation Just Cause is declared concluded on the thirty-first of January. The isthmus that Ferdinand de Lesseps and Gustave Eiffel contracted to cut in the 1880s, and that William Paterson tried to settle in 1698, is now a country with no army at all, run by a president sworn in on a foreign base while its capital's oldest working-class quarter was burning.
stops.quote: This is an exception to diplomatic immunity. We've indicted him as a drug dealer... you must understand that having lost American lives to restore democracy in Panama, we cannot allow Noriega to go to any other country than the United States.
stops.quote_source: James Baker, letter to the Vatican, December 1989; quoted in Meena Bose and Rosanna Perotti, From Cold War to New World Order (Greenwood Press, 2002), p. 181
suggested_refs: Department of Defense flight records for the transfer of 3-4 January 1990
sources: US Department of Defense statements, January 1990

stops.name: Homestead, landing as cargo
stops.date_confidence: attested.
stops.campa: The military flight lands in Florida and he stands on United States soil for the first time as a prisoner rather than as an asset. The same government that paid him from 1955 and put him on the regular payroll in 1971 now holds him under indictment for the years in between. Nothing in the record suggests anyone in Washington finds the sequence remarkable at the time. He is thirty-five years an informant and one day a defendant, and both careers were run out of the same set of buildings.
suggested_refs: Press coverage of the arrival at Homestead Air Force Base, 4 January 1990
sources: Contemporaneous Associated Press and Miami Herald reporting, January 1990

stops.name: Miami, the federal prison
stops.date_confidence: the day after the landing; the exact transfer date is not documented in the sources reached. The facility is one site under two names, called MCC-Miami in the late 1980s and renamed FCI-Miami in June 1995, and the research pool wrongly carried it as two separate places.
stops.campa: He is held in southwest Miami-Dade, pending trial and then for two decades. Prisoner-of-war status brings him a television, exercise equipment and a separate wing, and Miami newspapers report the arrangements with heat. He is the only prisoner of war the United States is holding. The status is a concession made at the Nunciature gate and not easily withdrawn afterward, and it follows him through a criminal trial, a forty-year sentence, and an extradition fight that outlasts the sentence.
suggested_refs: Bureau of Prisons records for Noriega at MCC-Miami, later FCI-Miami

stops.name: Miami, the court
stops.date_confidence: the verdict falls on 9 April 1992 after a trial running from September 1991; the sentence of forty years follows on 10 July 1992.
stops.campa: A federal jury convicts him on eight of ten counts of drug trafficking, racketeering and money laundering after seven months of trial. In July he is sentenced to forty years. It is one of the first times an American court tries a foreign head of state fetched by an American army. The evidence includes the accounts at Abedi's bank, the testimony of traffickers, and the files of an agency that was employing him through the years in which the offences were committed.
suggested_refs: US v. Noriega, 746 F. Supp. 1506 (S.D. Fla. 1990) and the trial record

stops.name: Miami, the memoir
stops.date_confidence: the book is published in 1997; no month is recorded in the catalogue records consulted, so month and day default to the first.
stops.campa: Random House publishes America's Prisoner: The Memoirs of Manuel Noriega, written with the journalist Peter Eisner from inside federal custody. He denies the trafficking and the murder and presents himself as a nationalist caught between United States intelligence and Reagan-era policy in Central America. This research reached the catalogue record and not the text, so nothing from inside the book is quoted here. A second English edition is catalogued the year after, and no translations are recorded.
suggested_refs: America's Prisoner: The Memoirs of Manuel Noriega, Random House, 1997, ISBN 0679432272

stops.name: La Sante, Paris
stops.date_confidence: the extradition from the United States to France falls in April 2010; the exact day is reported differently in different accounts and is not settled here. His American sentence had reached its scheduled completion in 2007, when he was held for extradition rather than released.
stops.campa: The United States extradites him to France, which had convicted him in absentia in 1999 of laundering Colombian drug money through French banks. He is held at La Sante, in the fourteenth arrondissement, a prison inside the city. He is seventy-six by the earliest of the three years offered for his birth. Panama has asked for him too, so he is now a man three states want to hold, each for a different set of crimes committed in a different decade of the same life.
suggested_refs: The French in absentia conviction of 1999 and the extradition of April 2010

stops.name: Ile de la Cite, the Paris court
stops.date_confidence: the French court confirms the money-laundering conviction in July 2010; the day is approximate, and the coordinates are those of the historic Palais de Justice.
stops.campa: A Paris court confirms the conviction and the sentence of seven years. The money it describes moved through French banks in the 1980s out of the same accounts the Miami trial described, and the same institution, Abedi's, stands behind both halves. Two national courts on two continents convict the same man for the two ends of one transaction, eighteen years apart. He serves a year and a half in France before Panama's request succeeds and he is put on another aircraft.
suggested_refs: French judicial records of the July 2010 money-laundering judgment
sources: Le Monde and AFP reporting, July 2010

stops.name: El Renacer, Gamboa
stops.date_confidence: attested for December 2011; the eleventh is the date reported for his arrival in Panama.
stops.campa: France sends him home. He goes into El Renacer, a prison beside the canal in the forest at Gamboa, to serve sentences handed down in absentia during the 1990s: the murder of Hugo Spadafora, and other crimes of his own government. Twenty-two years after the invasion the isthmus tries him at last under its own law, in a building a short way from the locks Gustave Eiffel's company contracted to build in 1887. He is an old man and the country has had no army since him.
suggested_refs: El Renacer prison at Gamboa; the Panamanian in absentia sentences of the 1990s

stops.name: Los Angeles, the suit against the game
stops.date_confidence: the suit is filed in July 2014 and dismissed on 28 October 2014; the pin takes the dismissal.
stops.campa: From prison he sues Activision in a Los Angeles court over his appearance in Call of Duty: Black Ops II, where he is a kidnapping target and an enemy of the state, and asks for a share of the profits. The court dismisses the suit in October on First Amendment grounds. The last legal action of his life is an attempt to own his own image, brought by a man whose image was an instrument of United States government publicity from the day soldiers photographed the shelves of his house.
suggested_refs: Noriega v. Activision Blizzard, Los Angeles Superior Court, dismissed 28 October 2014

stops.name: Hospital Santo Tomas, the operation
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia dates the brain tumour surgery to 15 February 2017. The research pool's claim of a diagnosis in March 2017 cannot stand, since a diagnosis cannot follow its own operation; the date of diagnosis is unknown and is not pinned.
stops.campa: He is taken from prison to the public hospital in Calidonia for surgery to remove a brain tumour. There are complications: a haemorrhage, a stroke. He is a prisoner of the Panamanian state and remains one in the ward. The hospital stands about two kilometres from the ground where the Comandancia stood and the tenements burned, in a capital that has spent twenty-seven years arguing about how many of its own people died there in a single night and has not agreed yet.
suggested_refs: Hospital Santo Tomas, Calle 36, Calidonia, Panama City

stops.name: Hospital Santo Tomas, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested. His age is reported as eighty-three, which fits the earliest of the three years offered for his birth.
stops.campa: He dies in the hospital on the twenty-ninth of May, aged eighty-three, of the cerebral haemorrhage that followed the surgery. He has been in custody without a break since the third of January 1990, in three countries, under four sets of sentences. The man who could not be found for four days in December 1989 dies at a fixed address, in the city where three different years are given for his birth and no document has ever settled which of them is right.
suggested_refs: Panamanian government statement on Noriega's death, 29 May 2017
sources: New York Times and Associated Press obituaries, May 2017

stops.name: Panama City, the urn
stops.date_confidence: month only. The cremation follows the death in late May or early June 2017; no date is recorded in the sources reached, so the day defaults to the first.
stops.campa: The body is cremated in a private family ceremony. There is no state funeral, no public grave and no marked tomb, and the ashes go to his widow Felicidad Sieiro de Noriega in an urn whose later whereabouts nothing reached in this research records. This same coordinate carried him from intelligence chief to commander to Maximum Leader to the first hour of the invasion that ended him. The man who ruled the isthmus for six years leaves it no place to visit.
suggested_refs: The private cremation of May-June 2017; no public grave exists
